questions.problem:
Find a Cartesian equation of the osculating plane for the curve $r(t)$ at the point where $t=1,$ given that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =-6t\,i+3{t}^{2}\,j+{t}^{3}\,k \\ T(t) & =\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+2}(-2\,i+2t\,j+{t}^{2}\,k) \\ N(t) & =\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+2}[2t\,i+(2-{t}^{2})\,j+2t\,k].\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the unit tangent and the principal normal at the point where $t=1$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}T(1) & =\frac{1}{(1)^{2}+2}(-2\,i+2(1)\,j+(1)^{2}\,k)=\frac{1}{3}(-2\,i+2\,j+k) \\ N(1) & =\frac{1}{(1)^{2}+2}[2(1)\,i+(2-(1)^{2})\,j+2(1)\,k]=\frac{1}{3}[2\,i+j+2\,k].\end{aligned}
$$

Also, the position vector of the point where $t=1$ is

$$
p=r(1)=-6(1)\,i+3(1)^{2}\,j+(1)^{3}\,k=⟨-6,3,1⟩.
$$

Now, we need to find a vector that's perpendicular to the osculating plane. To do that, we use the cross product of the unit tangent $T(1)$ and the principal normal $N(1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(1)\times N(1) & =(\frac{1}{3}(-2\,i+2\,j+k))\times (\frac{1}{3}[2\,i+j+2\,k]) \\  & =(\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{3})\cdot \left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -2 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}(3\,i+6\,j-6\,k)\end{aligned}
$$

Since we are interested only in the direction of the above vector, let's write our perpendicular vector $n$ as 

$$
n=3\cdot (T(1)\times N(1))=i+2\,j-2\,k=⟨1,2,-2⟩.
$$

Finally, let $⟨x,y,z⟩$ denote the position vector of a point on the osculating plane. Since the plane is perpendicular to $n$ and passes through the tip of the position vector $p$, its Cartesian equation can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}(⟨x,y,z⟩-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n-p\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨1,2,-2⟩ & =⟨-6,3,1⟩\cdot ⟨1,2,-2⟩ \\ 1\cdot x+2\cdot y+(-2)\cdot z & =-2 \\ x+2y-2z+2 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the equation of the osculating plane (in parametric form) for a curve $r(t)$ at the point $P(0,1,0)$ where $t=1$, given that

$$
T(1)=\frac{1}{5}(3\,i+4\,k),\,N(1)=j.
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the position vector of the point $P(0,1,0)$ is $r(1)=j.$

The osculating plane passes through the point that is at the tip of the vector $r(1).$ The vectors $T(1)$ and $N(1)$ are parallel to this plane. Therefore, the equation of the plane (in parametric form) can be written as

$$
R(s,u)=r(1)+s\,T(1)+u\,N(1),\,s,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

 

Hence, the equation of the osculating plane at the point $(0,1,0)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s,u) & =r(1)+s\,T(1)+u\,N(1) \\  & =j+\frac{s}{5}(3\,i+4\,k)+u(j) \\  & =\frac{3s}{5}\,i+(1+u)\,j+\frac{4s}{5}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the shortest distance between the origin and the osculating plane for the curve $r(t)$ at the point $P(1,3,2)$ where $t=-1$, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(-1)=k,\,N(-1)=i.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the position vector of the point $P(1,3,2)$ is $p=i+3\,j+2\,k.$

We need to find a vector that's perpendicular to the osculating plane. To do that, we use the cross product of the unit tangent $T(-1)$ and the principal normal $N(-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =T(-1)\times N(-1) \\  & =k\times i \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the shortest distance between our plane and the origin is given by

$$
d=\frac{|(p-0)\cdot n|}{‖n‖}=\frac{|p\cdot n|}{‖n‖}=|p\cdot n|,
$$

since $‖n‖=1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|p\cdot n| \\  & =|(i+3\,j+2\,k)\cdot j| \\  & =|0+3+0| \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the osculating plane for a curve $r(t)$ at the point $P(5,2,1)$ where $t=3,$ given that

$$
T(3)=\frac{1}{5}(3\,i+4\,j),\,N(3)=\frac{1}{5}(4\,i-3\,j).
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the position vector of the point $P(5,2,1)$ is $p=⟨5,2,1⟩.$

To find the equation of the osculating plane, we need to find a vector that's perpendicular to it. To do that, we find the cross product of the unit tangent $T(3)$ and the principal normal $N(3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(3)\times N(3) & =\frac{1}{5}(3\,i+4\,j)\times \frac{1}{5}(4\,i-3\,j) \\  & =\frac{1}{25}\cdot \left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 3 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{25}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ -3 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 4 & -3\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{25}(-25\,k) \\  & =-k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our perpendicular vector $n$ is 

$$
n=T(3)\times N(3)=-k=⟨0,0,-1⟩.
$$

Finally, let $⟨x,y,z⟩$ denote the position vector of a general point on the osculating plane. Since the plane is perpendicular to $n$ and passes through the tip of the position vector $p$, its Cartesian equation can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}(⟨x,y,z⟩-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n-p\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,-1⟩ & =⟨5,2,1⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,-1⟩ \\ x(0)+y(0)+z(-1) & =5(0)+2(0)+1(-1) \\ 0+0-z & =0+0-1 \\ z-1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the shortest distance between the origin and the osculating plane for the curve $r(t)$ at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ given that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-t⟩ \\ T(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-1⟩ \\ N(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the unit tangent and the principal normal at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2},\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2},-1⟩=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨0,-1,-1⟩ \\ N(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2},-\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2},0⟩=⟨-1,0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, the position vector of the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ is

$$
p=r(\frac{\pi }{2})=⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2},\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2},\,-\frac{\pi }{2}⟩=⟨2,0,-\frac{\pi }{2}⟩.
$$

Now, we need to find a vector that's perpendicular to the osculating plane. To do that, we use the cross product of the unit tangent $T(\frac{\pi }{2})$ and the principal normal $N(\frac{\pi }{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\frac{\pi }{2})\times N(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨0,-1,-1⟩\times ⟨-1,0,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & -1 & -1 \\ -1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(j-k) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨0,1,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the shortest distance between our plane and the origin is given by

$$
d=\frac{|(p-0)\cdot n|}{‖n‖}=\frac{|p\cdot n|}{‖n‖}=|p\cdot n|,
$$

since $‖n‖=1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|p\cdot n| \\  & =|⟨2,0,-\frac{\pi }{2}⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨0,1,-1⟩| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}|0+0+\frac{\pi }{2}| \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
